title: Not quite eye to A.I.: student and teacher perspectives on the use of generative artificial intelligence in the writing process
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper examines how students and teachers view the appropriate use of generative AI (GenAI), specifically ChatGPT, across stages of the writing process. The authors focus on a practical question emerging from the rapid adoption of large language models in education: when is AI support acceptable, and when does it become inappropriate or dishonest? Rather than testing whether GenAI improves writing outcomes, the study investigates stakeholder perceptions of acceptable use in educational writing tasks.

The intervention/approach studied was a questionnaire built around six writing-process tasks: brainstorming, outlining, writing, revising, providing feedback, and evaluating. Participants read sample ChatGPT prompts and outputs for each task and rated four divisions of use: using AI when already competent, using AI as an idea/model generator, submitting AI output with disclosure, and submitting AI output without disclosure. The sample included 158 university students and 68 teachers, mostly undergraduates and higher-education educators, recruited from a U.S. public research university and multiple institutions worldwide. The teacher sample included only a small number of K-12 educators, but the study itself was primarily centered on higher education.

The main findings were that students and teachers broadly agreed that GenAI is most acceptable when it supports early-stage writing tasks or helps users model ideas without replacing their own work. Using GenAI to complete writing tasks, especially without disclosure, was seen as least acceptable by both groups. Some differences emerged: students were generally more accepting than teachers of undisclosed or directly submitted AI-assisted writing, while teachers were more accepting than students of using AI for feedback and evaluation as a model. The study concludes that institutions need explicit AI policies and teacher professional development, because nearly all respondents reported little or no training and little institutional guidance on acceptable AI use.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot / large language model interface used to generate text, outlines, revisions, feedback, and evaluations from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper used ChatGPT (GPT-3.5-turbo) to generate example outputs for brainstorming, outlining, essay writing, revision, feedback, and evaluation prompts, and surveyed student/teacher perceptions of the appropriateness of these uses in the writing process.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a cross-sectional survey and perception study, not an outcome study of K-12 reading or literacy achievement. It does not test whether ChatGPT improves learner outcomes relative to business-as-usual or non-AI supports.
impact_tier_rationale: No direct impact on reading/literacy outcomes was measured. The paper reports attitudes about acceptable use in writing, so there is no evidence of learning gains or losses to rate for impact.
